data.Documented value: Mandatory and voluntary disclosures in GCC listed firms

The aim of this study is to investigate empirically the extent of mandatory disclosure with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs) and the level of voluntary disclosure by firms in the Gulf Co-Operation Council (GCC) member states — namely, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) — over the period 2010 to 2013, and to explain why some firms disclose more than others. It aims to investigate the determinants of mandatory disclosure and voluntary disclosure in the annual reports of GCC listed firms. It seeks to assess the relationship between a number of firm-specific characteristics such as corporate characteristics, ownership structure factors, corporate governance factors and cultural factors (manager’s personal characteristics) and the extent of mandatory and voluntary disclosures. In addition, the impact of voluntary disclosure level on mandatory disclosure level, the impact of mandatory disclosure level on voluntary disclosure level and sub-sample country groups.The extent of mandatory disclosure and the level of voluntary disclosure are examined using two different disclosure indices. The former disclosure index contains 325 mandatory disclosure items and the latter disclosure index comprises 129 voluntary disclosure items. The empirical approach is applied to the financial statements of 120 listed firms. Multivariate regression analysis is employed to explore the relationships between the extent of mandatory and voluntary disclosures and firm characteristics of the firms and year dummy variables. The firm characteristics include corporate characteristics, ownership structure factors, corporate governance factors and cultural factors (managers’ personal characteristics). In addition, to the impact of voluntary disclosure level on mandatory disclosure level, the impact of mandatory disclosure level on voluntary disclosure level and sub-sample country groups.The average level of mandatory disclosure requirements with the 24 IFRSs investigated across firms and years was 0.73, with a range from 61% to 87%. The level of mandatory disclosure increased from 0.71 in 2010 to 0.73 in 2013, indicating that the level of mandatory disclosure has been improving in the region over the study period. However, no firm throughout the study period fully satisfied the benchmark index created. The level of mandatory disclosure varies across the GCC listed firms. The highest average mandatory disclosure level for all years was in the UAE (0.77) followed by Qatar (0.76) Kuwait (0.73) Oman (0.71), Saudi Arabia (0.71) and Bahrain (0.69).Several firm characteristics helped to explain the level of mandatory disclosure.

sections.heading: Mandatory and voluntary disclosures in GCC listed firms
paragraphs: ### Mandatory and Voluntary Disclosures in GCC Listed Firms [[S2|UWE Research Repository UWE Bristol]] The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states, including Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, have a unique regulatory environment that influences the extent of mandatory and voluntary disclosures in their listed firms. This study, conducted by UWE Research Repository, aims to empirically investigate the extent of mandatory disclosure with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs) and the level of voluntary disclosure by firms in the GCC member states over the period 2010 to 2013. The research seeks to explain why some firms disclose more than others and to assess the relationship between firm-specific characteristics and the extent of mandatory and voluntary disclosures. [[S2|UWE Research Repository UWE Bristol]] The study employs two different disclosure indices: a mandatory disclosure index with 325 items and a voluntary disclosure index with 129 items.

The empirical approach is applied to the financial statements of 120 listed firms, employing multivariate regression analysis to explore the relationships between the extent of mandatory and voluntary disclosures and firm characteristics such as corporate characteristics, ownership structure factors, corporate governance factors, and cultural factors (managers' personal characteristics). [[S2|UWE Research Repository UWE Bristol]] The findings indicate that the level of mandatory disclosure has been improving over the study period, with an average level of 0.73 across firms and years, ranging from 61% to 87%. This suggests that the level of mandatory disclosure has been improving in the region over the period 2010 to 2013. However, no firm throughout the study period fully satisfied the benchmark index created, indicating that there is still room for improvement in mandatory disclosure practices.

[[S2|UWE Research Repository UWE Bristol]] The study also examines the impact of voluntary disclosure level on mandatory disclosure level, the impact of mandatory disclosure level on voluntary disclosure level, and sub-sample country groups. The research finds that the average level of mandatory disclosure requirements with the 24 IFRSs investigated across firms and years was 0.73, with a range from 61% to 87%. The level of mandatory disclosure increased from 0.71 in 2010 to 0.73 in 2013, indicating that the level of mandatory disclosure has been improving in the region over the study period. [[S2|UWE Research Repository UWE Bristol]] However, the research also notes that some firms disclose more than others, suggesting that there is a difference in disclosure practices among firms.

paragraphs: ### Profit Warnings from UK Listed Firms [[S3|Journal of Competitiveness]] In recent years, the financial landscape has become increasingly volatile, with global capital markets experiencing heightened uncertainty. Recognizing the importance of understanding not just the causes of stock price crash risk but also the economic consequences thereof, a study has been conducted to explore the impact of crash risk exposure on corporate financial distress. This research, based on financial data of 11,336 A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2014 to 2023, employs a logit regression model to investigate the relationship between crash risk exposure and financial distress two years later. [[S3|Journal of Competitiveness]] The findings indicate that increased crash risk exposure significantly promotes the occurrence of financial distress.

Mechanism analysis reveals that heightened crash risk exposure deteriorates firms' financing conditions by intensifying financing constraints, increasing debt financing costs, and reducing institutional ownership, thereby exacerbating financial distress. A heterogeneity analysis further shows that the effect of increased crash risk exposure on financial distress is more pronounced in large firms and in the post-2018 period. [[S3|Journal of Competitiveness]] This study enriches research on corporate risk management and provides new insights for effectively preventing financial distress and enhancing firm competitiveness. The research underscores the importance of understanding the economic consequences of crash risk exposure, which can help firms better respond to black swan events.

sections.heading: Forecasting financial distress in listed Chinese construction firms: leveraging ensemble
paragraphs: ### Forecasting Financial Distress in Listed Chinese Construction Firms: Leveraging Ensemble Learning and Non-Financial Variables [[S4|Construction Management and Economics]] Predicting financial distress and early warnings in listed Chinese construction firms is crucial for mitigating potential crises. While financial ratios are commonly used, non-financial information remains underexplored, with limited empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness in enhancing predictive accuracy. This study presents a model that integrates accounting variables, firm characteristics, construction market dynamics, and macroeconomic indicators to predict the probability of failure one to two years in advance. The model employs a soft voting-based ensemble algorithm, refined financial ratios through the Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV) algorithm, and dataset balancing via Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique + Tomek Link (SMOTETomek).

The results indicate that the predictive performance of the soft voting ensemble model outperforms all single classifiers across all combinations of input variables and prediction years. Incorporating non-financial variables, such as firm characteristics, construction market dynamics, and macroeconomic indicators, further enhances the model's accuracy. The proposed model can effectively help stakeholders mitigate the risks associated with the financial distress of construction companies before the project implementation phase. [[S4|Construction Management and Economics]] ### Seasonal Affective Disorder and Investors' Response to Profit Warnings [[S4|Construction Management and Economics]] Investors' response to profit warnings is influenced by seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a medical condition characterized by a depressed mood during times of low daylight.

The study examines abnormal returns caused by profit warnings and finds that both positive and negative profit warnings generate significant abnormal returns on the announcement day. Investors have more difficulty evaluating negative profit warnings than positive profit warnings. The results suggest that the size, MB ratio, or analyst recommendations do not affect investors' response. However, the study finds differences in how investors respond to positive or negative profit warnings.

Specifically, the risk of the company affects the immediate response to negative profit warnings, while the number of previous profit warnings affects the post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) of positive profit warnings. The main interest of this thesis is the effect of SAD on investors' response to profit warnings. The immediate response to positive profit warnings is lower during the SAD season, supporting the hypothesis of heightened risk aversion. Moreover, the PEAD of negative profit warnings is higher during the SAD season, supporting the SAD hypothesis.
The findings imply that these effects are mainly driven by the fall.

sections.heading: Cross‐border information transfers: Evidence from profit warnings issued by European
paragraphs: ### Profit Warnings from UK-Listed Firms [[S5|Accounting and Business Research]] In recent years, UK-listed firms have been issuing more profit warnings, a trend that has been observed across European countries. This phenomenon is not just an isolated incident but a reflection of broader economic and regulatory changes affecting the financial landscape. The evidence presented in the paper "Cross-Border Information Transfers: Evidence from Profit Warnings Issued by European Firms" by S5 Accounting and Business Research suggests that negative earnings surprises disclosed by firms in one country can significantly impact investors' perceptions of comparable non-announcing firms in other countries. This cross-border effect is consistent with domestic transfers, indicating that firms are using information from their domestic markets to influence perceptions in international markets.

[[S5|Accounting and Business Research]] The study's findings are particularly relevant given the increasing interconnectedness of global markets. As firms operate across borders, they are exposed to different regulatory environments and market conditions. This interconnectedness has led to a greater need for cross-border information sharing and transfer, which can influence financial decisions and investor perceptions. The paper's evidence supports the notion that firms are using profit warnings as a means to communicate with investors about their financial health, thereby affecting the market perception of their international counterparts.

[[S5|Accounting and Business Research]] The mechanism behind this cross-border effect is complex and multifaceted. It involves the interaction of domestic and international markets, regulatory frameworks, and investor behavior. The study's findings provide valuable insights into how firms are using profit warnings as a tool for cross-border communication and influence. This information can be crucial for investors and regulators, as it highlights the potential impact of domestic market conditions on international firms and vice versa.

[[S5|Accounting and Business Research]] The limitations of this research are significant. The sample size of 29 European countries is relatively small, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, the study does not provide a comprehensive explanation of the underlying mechanisms that drive cross-border information transfers. While the paper offers some explanations, it does not fully address the complexities involved in cross-border financial communication.

[[S5|Accounting and Business Research]] In conclusion, the trend of UK-listed firms issuing more profit warnings is a concerning development that underscores the interconnectedness of global markets. This phenomenon is not just an isolated incident but a reflection of broader economic and regulatory changes.

sections.heading: Stock Returns Following Profit Warnings
paragraphs: ### Stock Returns Following Profit Warnings [[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] Stock returns following profit warnings can offer valuable insights into the behavior of investors and the market's reaction to financial information. According to the research conducted by Open Research Exeter (University of Exeter), abnormal returns are estimated on stocks for two years following a profit warning. The findings reveal that qualitative warnings, issued in the first three months, result in negative abnormal returns of -9.6%, while quantitative warnings, issued twelve months after the warning, yield positive abnormal returns of 4.6%. [[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] These results suggest that investors may be more cautious after qualitative warnings, leading to a decrease in stock returns, whereas quantitative warnings might indicate a more optimistic outlook, resulting in an increase in returns.

This mechanism can be explained by the behavioral finance model, which posits that investors may react differently to positive and negative information. The model predicts that investors might be more inclined to buy stocks following a qualitative warning, expecting a positive outcome, while they might be more cautious after a quantitative warning, fearing the opposite. [[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] ### Corporate Financial Distress of Industry Level Listings in Vietnam [[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] The study by the Journal of risk and financial management examines the corporate financial distress of listed firms in Vietnam over the past decade, focusing on the industry level. The research employs the logit regression technique to estimate alternative models based on accounting and market factors.

The analysis also includes selected macroeconomic factors to further enhance the predictive power of the models. [[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] The empirical findings confirm that the corporate financial distress prediction model, which includes accounting factors with macroeconomic indicators, performs much better than alternative models. This suggests that accounting factors play a crucial role in predicting corporate financial distress, especially in the context of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). The research also highlights the impact of the GFC on various sectors, with the Health & Education sector demonstrating the most impressive recovery post-GFC, and the Utilities sector recording a dramatic increase in bankruptcies post-GFC.

[[S6|Open Research Exeter University of Exeter]] The evidence provided in this study underscores the importance of considering the industry level when analyzing corporate financial distress, as it can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing financial distress.

sections.heading: Seasonal affective disorder and investors' response to profit warnings
paragraphs: ### Seasonal Affective Disorder and Investors' Response to Profit Warnings [[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a medical condition characterized by a depressed mood during times of low daylight. This phenomenon has a significant impact on investors' response to profit warnings from UK-listed firms. The research examines how SAD affects investors' reaction to profit warnings, particularly focusing on abnormal returns and investor evaluation of positive and negative profit warnings. [[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] The first part of the research explores abnormal returns caused by profit warnings.

The study finds that both positive and negative profit warnings generate significant abnormal returns on the announcement day. Additionally, investors have more difficulty evaluating negative profit warnings than positive ones. The results imply that the size, market capitalization ratio, or analyst recommendations do not influence investors' response. However, the research identifies differences in how investors respond to positive and negative profit warnings.

[[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] In the seventh section’s third paragraph, the first evidence point for Seasonal affective disorder and investors' response to profit warnings is that specifically, the risk of the company affects the immediate response to negative profit warnings, while the number of previous profit warnings affects the post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) of positive profit warnings. [[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] The main interest of this thesis is to investigate the effect of SAD on investors' response to profit warnings. The immediate response to positive profit warnings is lower during the SAD season, which supports the hypothesis about heightened risk aversion. Moreover, the PEAD of negative profit warnings is higher during the SAD season, which also supports the SAD hypothesis.

The research findings suggest that these effects are mainly driven by the fall. Interestingly, the study finds that SAD does not affect the immediate response to negative profit warnings or the PEAD of positive profit warnings. This suggests that these two findings are explained by the ostrich effect and negativity bias, respectively. [[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] ### COVID-19 Profit Warnings: Delivering Bad News in a Time of Crisis [[S7|Osuva University of Vaasa]] The research on COVID-19 profit warnings examines the quality of these disclosures in the context of a worldwide crisis.

The study develops a genre-based typology/analytical framework for assessing COVID-19 profit warnings' quality, comprising four profit warning/forecast quality characteristics and eight profit warning/forecast disclosures.

paragraphs: ### Profit Warnings from UK-Listed Firms [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] In recent times, profit warnings from UK-listed firms have reached their highest level in two years, driven by the ongoing Iran war. This development has sparked significant concern among investors and analysts alike. The war has heightened costs, leading to financial instability and uncertainty in the market. As a result, firms are now more cautious about their financial statements, leading to increased profit warnings.

[[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] ### Influence of Leverage, Liquidity, and Firm Value [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] This research examines the influence of leverage, liquidity, and company value on non-financial business enterprises listed in the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) in Kenya. The study aims to provide solutions for the declining trend in firm value, which has been observed over the years. [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] ### Methodology [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] The research utilized panel data from secondary sources, including annual reports of NSE-listed non-financial firms from 2016 to 2022. The methodology involved panel regression analysis and Pearson's product moment correlation analysis to determine the relationship between leverage, liquidity, and firm value.

[[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] ### Findings [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] The panel regression results indicated that both leverage (p=0.003, <0.05) and liquidity (p=0.002, <0.05) had a statistically significant positive effect on firm value. The study concluded that both leverage and liquidity have a very strong positive relationship with firm value. High liquidity levels led to increased trading activity and higher demand for a company's shares, while leverage amplified both the potential returns and risks for a company. [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] ### Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice, and Policy [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] The research advocates that companies should expand their debt levels to potentially raise their firm value.

This finding is significant as it provides a practical solution to the declining trend in firm value observed over the years. [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] ### Conclusion [[S1|International Journal of Finance and Accounting]] The profit warnings from UK-listed firms, driven by the Iran war, have highlighted the importance of leverage, liquidity, and firm value in the financial health of non-financial businesses.

The issue is particularly pronounced in the healthcare and education sectors, where companies are struggling to maintain profitability amidst challenging market conditions. This trend is not isolated to the UK; it is also evident in other countries, including Vietnam, where the corporate financial distress of industry-level listings has been a topic of significant interest.

During the GFC (2007–2009), the Health & Education sector demonstrated the most impressive recovery post-GFC, with a dramatic increase in bankruptcies post-GFC. This recovery was particularly pronounced in the Utilities sector, which experienced a significant increase in bankruptcies post-GFC. The findings underscore the importance of understanding the specific industries and sectors affected by financial distress and the mechanisms that contribute to their recovery or deterioration.

paragraphs: ### Profit Warnings from UK-Listed Firms: Delivering Bad News in a Time of Crisis [[S3|The British Accounting Review]] In the wake of the global pandemic, UK-listed firms have been compelled to deliver profit warnings, a practice that has become increasingly important in the context of the 2020 COVID-19 exogenous shock. These warnings serve as a distinctive corporate communication genre, providing a platform for companies to deliver bad news in a time of crisis. The research, "COVID-19 Profit Warnings: Delivering Bad News in a Time of Crisis," by the British Accounting Review, develops a genre-based typology/analytical framework for assessing the quality of these profit warnings. The study analyzes the content of 160 profit-warning documents, culminating in a disclosure quality score/index.

[[S3|The British Accounting Review]] The research finds that companies tend to regress to silence when investors most need guidance, reflecting poor-quality disclosure. The study identifies two significant variables influencing disclosure quality: profit warnings disclosed following Financial Reporting Council guidance are of higher quality, and quality varies by industry. The research also explores the concept of faux disclosure, where boards of directors may use ambiguous language to tick-box compliance with market abuse regulations, potentially masking minimal regulatory guidance. [[S3|The British Accounting Review]] The paper concludes with recommendations for policymakers to enhance the quality of these crucial corporate documents.

Policymakers should consider improving the regulatory framework to ensure that companies are held accountable for their disclosures, thereby enhancing the transparency and reliability of financial reporting. This includes providing clearer guidance on the interpretation of financial statements and the use of standardized reporting formats.
